claim: Hallmark social activities of humans, such as cooperation and cultural learning, involve eye-gaze signaling through joint attentional interaction and ostensive communication.
source: Hallmark social activities of humans, such as cooperation and cultural learning, involve eye-gaze signaling through joint attentional interaction and ostensive communication.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about human social behavior and communication.

claim: The gaze-signaling hypothesis posits that humans evolved unique external eye morphologies, including uniformly white sclera, to enhance the visibility of eye-gaze for conspecifics.
source: The gaze-signaling and related cooperative-eye hypotheses posit that humans evolved unique external eye morphologies, including uniformly white sclera (the whites of the eye), to enhance the visibility of eye-gaze for conspecifics.
evidence: This claim references the gaze-signaling hypothesis from the literature.

claim: Both humans and chimpanzees discriminated eye-gaze directions of humans better than those of chimpanzees, particularly in visually challenging conditions.
source: We found that both humans and chimpanzees discriminated eye-gaze directions of humans better than those of chimpanzees, particularly in visually challenging conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study's tests with human and chimpanzee participants.

claim: Participants of both species discriminated the eye-gaze directions of chimpanzees better when the contrast polarity of the chimpanzee eye was reversed compared to when it was normal.
source: Also, participants of both species discriminated the eye-gaze directions of chimpanzees better when the contrast polarity of the chimpanzee eye was reversed compared to when it was normal; namely, when the chimpanzee eye has human-like white sclera and a darker iris.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the study comparing normal and reversed contrast polarity conditions.

claim: Uniform whiteness in the sclera facilitates the visibility of eye-gaze direction even across species.
source: Uniform whiteness in the sclera thus facilitates the visibility of eye-gaze direction even across species.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data showing improved performance with white sclera in both human and chimpanzee participants.

claim: Humans excel at detecting another's direct gaze and following another's gaze directions from early infancy.
source: Humans excel at detecting another's direct gaze and following another's gaze directions from early infancy (Farroni et al., 2002; Farroni et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research studies.

claim: During social interactions, humans exchange communicative intentions with one another via eye contact.
source: Moreover, during social interactions, humans exchange communicative intentions with one another via eye contact (Senju and Johnson, 2009; Kleinke, 1986), and an experience of being watched by another affects one's reputational concerns (Bateson et al., 2006; Engelmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nonhuman great apes excel at detecting another's direct gaze.
source: Comparative studies have found that closely related species such as nonhuman great apes also excel at detecting another's direct gaze (Myowa-Yamakoshi et al., 2003)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to comparative studies.

claim: Nonhuman great apes excel at following another's gaze directions.
source: Comparative studies have found that closely related species such as nonhuman great apes also excel at detecting another's direct gaze (Myowa-Yamakoshi et al., 2003) and following another's gaze directions (Bräuer et al., 2005; Okamoto et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative studies.

claim: Nonhuman great apes adjust their gaze-following behaviors flexibly and cognitively.
source: and adjust their gaze-following behaviors flexibly and cognitively (Kano and Call, 2014; Okamoto-Barth et al., 2007; Povinelli and Eddy, 1996; Tomasello et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Nonhuman great apes make eye contact with other individuals at critical moments of social interactions, such as when requesting food from an experimenter.
source: Moreover, they make eye contact with other individuals at critical moments of social interactions, such as when requesting food from an experimenter (Gomez, 1996) and initiating affiliative social interactions with conspecifics (Heesen et al., 2021; Yamagiwa, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: While humans primarily relied on another's eye-directional cues in gaze-following/cueing experiments, nonhuman apes relied on head-directional rather than eye-directional cues.
source: For example, in the gaze-following/cueing experiments, while humans primarily relied on another's eye-directional cues, nonhuman apes relied on head-directional rather than eye-directional cues (Tomasello et al., 2007; Tomonaga, 2007, but see Povinelli and Eddy, 1996; Deaner and Platt, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Reliance on eye-directional rather than head-directional cues indicates one's inclination/ability to identify a specific spot that another's foveae are directing at, rather than a large area that another's field of view covers.
source: In general, reliance on eye-directional rather than head-directional cues indicates one's inclination/ability to identify a specific spot that another's foveae are directing at, rather than a large area that another's field of view covers.
evidence: This claim is based on logical inference about the functional differences between eye-directional and head-directional cues.

claim: While both human infants and nonhuman apes alternately looked at both the interaction partner's face and the focused object during joint-attentional interactions, nonhuman apes made only brief looks to the interaction partner's face while human infants made more long-lasting looks.
source: Relatedly, a previous study observed that, while both human infants and nonhuman apes alternately looked at both the interaction partner's face and the focused object during joint-attentional interactions, nonhuman apes made only brief looks to the interaction partner's face while human infants made more long-lasting looks (Carpenter and Tomasello, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Human infants responded to an agent's eye contact as if they interpreted it as an ostensive signal preceding referential information in a communicative gaze-following task.
source: Furthermore, in a communicative gaze-following task, while human infants responded to an agent's eye contact as if they interpreted it as an ostensive signal preceding referential information (Senju and Csibra, 2008; Okumura et al., 2020; but see Gredebäck et al., 2018), great apes did not show any evidence supporting this understanding (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Great apes did not show any evidence supporting the understanding that eye contact is an ostensive signal preceding referential information in a communicative gaze-following task.
source: Furthermore, in a communicative gaze-following task, while human infants responded to an agent's eye contact as if they interpreted it as an ostensive signal preceding referential information (Senju and Csibra, 2008; Okumura et al., 2020; but see Gredebäck et al., 2018), great apes did not show any evidence supporting this understanding (Kano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The gaze-signaling hypothesis is based on comparative analyses showing that uniformly white sclera is a unique feature of the human eye among primates.
source: This hypothesis is based on comparative analyses showing that (1) uniformly white sclera is a unique feature of the human eye among primates and that (2) the human eye is horizontally more elongated, and the human sclera is horizontally more exposed compared to other primates' eyes (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 2001; Kobayashi and Kohshima, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative analyses.

claim: The human eye is horizontally more elongated, and the human sclera is horizontally more exposed compared to other primates' eyes.
source: This hypothesis is based on comparative analyses showing that (1) uniformly white sclera is a unique feature of the human eye among primates and that (2) the human eye is horizontally more elongated, and the human sclera is horizontally more exposed compared to other primates' eyes (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 2001; Kobayashi and Kohshima, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to comparative analyses.

claim: The cooperative-eye hypothesis proposes that humans evolved morphological features of the eye as well as a special sensitivity to these features to facilitate joint-attentional and communicative interactions in a cooperative context.
source: The cooperative-eye hypothesis (Tomasello et al., 2007) extended this gaze-signaling hypothesis based on the results from their gaze-following study, proposing that humans evolved these morphological features as well as a special sensitivity to these features to facilitate joint-attentional and communicative interactions in a cooperative context.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to the cooperative-eye hypothesis.

claim: Humans' white sclera signals not only gaze direction but also emotional cues in combination with fine musculatures around the eyes.
source: Others discussed that humans' white sclera not only signals gaze direction but also emotional cues in combination with fine musculatures around the eyes (Whalen et al., 2004; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Jessen and Grossmann, 2014), and also emotional and health-status cues by its color variations (Provine et al., 2013a; Provine et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Humans' white sclera signals emotional and health-status cues by its color variations.
source: Others discussed that humans' white sclera not only signals gaze direction but also emotional cues in combination with fine musculatures around the eyes (Whalen et al., 2004; Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Jessen and Grossmann, 2014), and also emotional and health-status cues by its color variations (Provine et al., 2013a; Provine et al., 2013b).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Typically developing human adults and children show basic preferences for an animal agent having white sclera.
source: Moreover, typically developing human adults and children show basic preferences for an animal agent having white sclera (Segal et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Recent quantitative morphological studies have challenged the gaze-signaling and cooperative-eye hypotheses by showing that certain eye features of humans are not necessarily unique among great ape species.
source: Despite the widespread popularity of the gaze-signaling and related cooperative-eye hypotheses in the literature, these hypotheses have been severely challenged by recent quantitative morphological studies showing that certain eye features of humans are not necessarily unique among great ape species (Mayhew and Gómez, 2015; Perea-García et al., 2019; Caspar et al., 2021; Mearing and Koops, 2021; Kano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent morphological studies.

claim: The sclera of humans is not necessarily more exposed than that of other great ape species.
source: Specifically, those studies have shown that (1) the sclera of humans is not necessarily more exposed than that of other great ape species (Mayhew and Gómez, 2015; Caspar et al., 2021; Kano et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: The color contrast/difference between the iris and the sclera is similar between humans and other great apes.
source: that (2) the color contrast/difference between the iris and the sclera is similar between humans and other great apes (Perea-García et al., 2019; Caspar et al., 2021; Mearing and Koops, 2021; Kano et al., 2021)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: There is substantial individual variation in the extent to which sclera is unpigmented among some nonhuman ape species.
source: and that (3) there is substantial individual variation in the extent to which sclera is unpigmented among some nonhuman ape species (Mayhew and Gómez, 2015; Caspar et al., 2021; Mearing and Koops, 2021; Kano et al., 2021; Perea García, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to morphological studies.

claim: One eye feature that both distinguishes humans from other great apes and contributes to the visibility of eye-gaze direction is uniform whiteness in humans' exposed sclera.
source: Given these new findings, one recent study suggested that one (and possibly only) eye feature that both distinguishes humans from other great apes and contributes to the visibility of eye-gaze direction is uniform whiteness in humans' exposed sclera; i.e., depigmentation all the way from the iris edge to the eye corners (Kano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Uniformly white sclera characterizes clear visibilities of both iris and eye-outline edges, which are the two essential features that contribute to the visibility of eye-gaze directions.
source: This previous study used image analysis and computer vision techniques and identified that uniformly white sclera characterizes clear visibilities of both iris and eye-outline edges – the two essential features that contribute to the visibility of eye-gaze directions (see Appendix 3—figure 1 for the illustration of this aspect).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study using image analysis and computer vision, and references a figure.

claim: The iris is highly visible in all great ape species.
source: More specifically, while the iris is highly visible in all great ape species, the visibility of eye-outline edges is limited in nonhuman apes because most nonhuman ape individuals have darker or more graded/patchy sclera colors compared to humans' sclera colors, which more easily blend into the adjacent skin/hair colors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from previous morphological studies.

claim: The visibility of eye-outline edges is limited in nonhuman apes because most nonhuman ape individuals have darker or more graded/patchy sclera colors compared to humans' sclera colors, which more easily blend into the adjacent skin/hair colors.
source: More specifically, while the iris is highly visible in all great ape species, the visibility of eye-outline edges is limited in nonhuman apes because most nonhuman ape individuals have darker or more graded/patchy sclera colors compared to humans' sclera colors, which more easily blend into the adjacent skin/hair colors.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from morphological observations.

claim: Nearly all human individuals have uniformly white sclera, which is clearly distinguished from the adjacent skin/hair colors around the eyes even when the eyes are viewed in visually challenging conditions.
source: On the other hand, nearly all human individuals have uniformly white sclera, which is clearly distinguished from the adjacent skin/hair colors around the eyes (irrespective of the skin color variations) even when the eyes are viewed in visually challenging conditions (e.g., shading, distancing).
evidence: This claim is based on morphological observations and inference.

claim: Reversing the contrast polarity of human eye images makes the judgment of gaze direction less accurate in human participants.
source: Ricciardelli et al., 2000 tested human participants in a gaze-discrimination task and found that reversing the contrast polarity of human eye images makes the judgment of gaze direction less accurate.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Gaze directions were more accurately judged in eyes having a positive (normal) contrast polarity (white sclera with a darker iris) than those having a negative (reversed) contrast polarity (black sclera with a bright iris) in human participants.
source: Specifically, the gaze directions were more accurately judged in eyes having a positive (normal) contrast polarity (white sclera with a darker iris) than those having a negative (reversed) contrast polarity (black sclera with a bright iris), even though these two eye images were composed of the same colors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Humans have perceptual expertise in positive contrast polarity of eyes.
source: Ricciardelli et al. thus suggested that humans have perceptual expertise in positive contrast polarity of eyes (see Itier et al., 2006; Yoshizaki and Kato, 2011 for related results).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Human participants detected faces with conspicuous sclera colors (white or lighter than the iris color) faster and more accurately than faces with inconspicuous sclera colors (similar or darker than the iris color).
source: Also, Yorzinski and Miller, 2020 tested human participants in a gaze-discrimination task in which the sclera colors of human faces were manipulated to be either conspicuous (white or lighter than the iris color) or inconspicuous (similar or darker than the iris color); human participants detected the faces with conspicuous sclera colors faster and more accurately.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: Humans' white sclera facilitates their gaze perception.
source: Yorzinski and Miller thus suggested that humans' white sclera facilitates their gaze perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A chimpanzee's task performance dropped when the contrast polarity of the eyes was reversed in stimulus human faces.
source: Tomonaga and Imura, 2010 tested whether a chimpanzee could be trained to discriminate eye-gaze directions of human facial images, and in one of their experimental conditions, they replicated the results from Ricciardelli et al., 2000. Specifically, they showed that the chimpanzee's task performance dropped when the contrast polarity of the eyes was reversed in the stimulus human faces.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous experimental study.

claim: No previous study adopted a fully crossed design for species comparison to examine the effect of sclera colors on primate gaze perception.
source: Critically, no previous study adopted a fully crossed design for species comparison to examine the effect of sclera colors on primate gaze perception; namely, a study design that presents the stimuli of both species to the participants of both species.
evidence: This claim is based on review of previous literature.

claim: Chimpanzees' eyes have relatively uniformly dark sclera and a bright iris, having a negative contrast polarity opposite to the positive contrast polarity that human eyes have.
source: Chimpanzees are a suitable species for this design because their eyes have relatively uniformly dark sclera and a bright iris, namely, having a negative contrast polarity opposite to the positive contrast polarity that human eyes have.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological knowledge about chimpanzee eyes.

claim: The contrast polarity of both species' eyes was reversed by inverting the lightness values of the eyeball images in the faces.
source: The contrast polarity of both species' eyes (only the eyeball regions) was reversed by inverting the lightness (or grayscale) values of the eyeball images in the faces (Figure 1A and Appendix 3—figure 3).
evidence: This claim describes the experimental manipulation performed in the study, with reference to figures.

claim: The manipulation of reversing contrast polarity created artificial white sclera in chimpanzee eyes and artificial dark sclera in human eyes, while not affecting the iris-sclera color differences in each species' eyes.
source: This manipulation created artificial white sclera in chimpanzee eyes and artificial dark sclera in human eyes, while not affecting the iris-sclera (or pupil-iris) color differences in each species' eyes.
evidence: This claim describes the result of the experimental manipulation.

claim: The strength of the visual signal generally depends on its degradation caused by natural noises.
source: Also, as the strength of the visual signal generally depends on its degradation caused by natural noises (Endler, 1990), we tested the robustness of eye-gaze signals against shading and distancing (Figure 1A), namely the simulated visual conditions where stimulus eyes were presented darker (in shadows) and smaller (in the distance), following a previous study on great ape eye color (Kano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to signal theory and references a figure.

claim: Human participants performed better in trials presenting the human stimuli than those presenting the chimpanzee stimuli in Experiment 1 of Study 1.
source: We tested the effect of stimulus level and species on participants' correct responses (correct, incorrect) in a binomial generalized linear mixed model (GLMM; see Appendix 1—table 1 for the formulas) and found that human participants performed better in trials presenting the human stimuli than those presenting the chimpanzee stimuli (χ2 = 37.08, df = 1, p<10–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Human participants' performance was worse in trials presenting smaller and more shaded stimuli in Experiment 1 of Study 1.
source: We also found that their performance was worse in trials presenting smaller and more shaded stimuli (χ2 = 45.85, df = 3, p<10–9; see Appendix 1—table 2 for the full GLMM results; Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references a figure.

claim: There was a significant three-way interaction effect between stimulus level, species, and contrast polarity on human participants' correct responses in Experiment 2 of Study 1.
source: We tested the effect of stimulus level, species, and contrast polarity on participants' correct responses in GLMM and found a significant three-way interaction effect between these factors (Figure 2B; χ2 = 17.57, df = 1, p<10–4; also see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data and references a figure.

claim: Human participants performed better in trials presenting the positive (reversed) eyes of chimpanzees than those presenting the negative (normal) eyes of chimpanzees.
source: Critically, we found that human participants performed better in trials presenting the positive (reversed) eyes of chimpanzees (i.e., the white sclera and a darker iris) than those presenting the negative (normal) eyes of chimpanzees (i.e., the dark sclera and a bright iris), while they performed worse in trials presenting the negative (reversed) eyes of humans than those presenting the positive (normal) eyes of humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Human participants performed worse in trials presenting the negative (reversed) eyes of humans than those presenting the positive (normal) eyes of humans.
source: Critically, we found that human participants performed better in trials presenting the positive (reversed) eyes of chimpanzees (i.e., the white sclera and a darker iris) than those presenting the negative (normal) eyes of chimpanzees (i.e., the dark sclera and a bright iris), while they performed worse in trials presenting the negative (reversed) eyes of humans than those presenting the positive (normal) eyes of humans.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Only three chimpanzees (Natsuki, Hatsuka, Pendesa) passed all the required training and participated in test phases of Study 2.
source: In Study 2, we began with training 10 chimpanzees. Only three (Natsuki, Hatsuka, Pendesa) passed all the required training and subsequently participated in test phases (see Appendix 2—table 1 for details about participants; also see Appendix 4—table 1 and Figure 1 for the number and performance of training sessions for each chimpanzee).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the training phase.

claim: All three chimpanzees in Experiment 1 of Study 2 performed significantly better for the human stimuli than the chimpanzee stimuli during the test phase.
source: We tested the effect of stimulus species in binomial GLMM on each chimpanzee's correct responses (correct, incorrect) during the test phase and found that all three chimpanzees performed significantly better for the human stimuli than the chimpanzee stimuli (Natsuki: χ2 = 8.28, df = 1, p=0.004; Hatsuka: χ2 = 9.50, df = 1, p=0.002; Pendesa: χ2 = 21.94, df = 1, p<10–5; also see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between stimulus species and phase in both Natsuki and Hatsuka when comparing Test A1 and Test B in Experiment 2 of Study 2.
source: We compared each chimpanzee's correct responses in target trials across Test A1 and Test B in GLMM and found a significant interaction effect between stimulus species and phase in both chimpanzees (Natsuki: χ2 = 34.61, df = 1, p<10–8; Hatsuka; χ2 = 8.39, df = 1, p=0.004; also see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was a significant interaction effect between stimulus species and phase in both Natsuki and Hatsuka when comparing Test B and Test A2 in Experiment 2 of Study 2.
source: We then compared each chimpanzee's performance across Test B and Test A2 and found a significant interaction effect between the two factors in both chimpanzees (Natsuki: χ2 = 37.04, df = 1, p<10–8; Hatsuka; χ2 = 33.75, df = 1, p<10–8).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Both chimpanzees' performance significantly increased from Test A1 to Test B and then decreased from Test B to Test A2 in trials presenting the chimpanzee stimuli.
source: Critically, we found that both chimpanzees' performance significantly increased from Test A1 (normal contrast polarity) to Test B (reversed contrast polarity) and then their performance decreased from Test B to Test A2 (normal contrast polarity) in trials presenting the chimpanzee stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Natsuki's performance significantly decreased from Test A1 to Test B and then increased from Test B to Test A2 in trials presenting the human stimuli.
source: Natsuki's performance significantly decreased from Test A1 to Test B and then increased from Test B to Test A2 in trials presenting the human stimuli.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: Hatsuka's performance did not significantly decrease from Test A1 to Test B but significantly increased from Test B to Test A2 in trials presenting the human stimuli.
source: Hatsuka's performance did not significantly decrease from Test A1 to Test B but significantly increased from Test B to Test A2 in those trials.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: The results revealed a striking advantage of eyes having positive contrast polarity in the gaze-discrimination performance of both human and chimpanzee participants.
source: Overall, these results revealed a striking advantage of eyes having positive contrast polarity, namely, the eyes of both species with the uniformly white sclera and a darker iris, in the gaze-discrimination performance of both human and chimpanzee participants.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The results supported H1 (perceptual advantage of uniformly white sclera).
source: Our results thus supported H1 (perceptual advantage of uniformly white sclera).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: Both human and chimpanzee eye-gaze directions are reliably discernible when those eyes were presented sufficiently large and bright.
source: We also found that, although both human and chimpanzee eye-gaze directions are reliably discernible when those eyes were presented sufficiently large and bright (i.e., L1–2 stimuli), the human eye-gaze directions were more discernible than the chimpanzee eye-gaze particularly when those eyes were presented smaller and more shaded (i.e., L3–4 stimuli).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The human eye-gaze directions were more discernible than the chimpanzee eye-gaze particularly when those eyes were presented smaller and more shaded.
source: We also found that, although both human and chimpanzee eye-gaze directions are reliably discernible when those eyes were presented sufficiently large and bright (i.e., L1–2 stimuli), the human eye-gaze directions were more discernible than the chimpanzee eye-gaze particularly when those eyes were presented smaller and more shaded (i.e., L3–4 stimuli).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: H2 (perceptual advantage of the iris-sclera color difference) cannot explain the overall patterns of the results.
source: Our alternative hypotheses (H2–5) cannot explain the overall patterns of our results. H2 (perceptual advantage of the iris-sclera color difference) cannot explain our results likely because it supposes clear visibility of only iris but not that of eye-outline edges, another critical feature that contributes to the visibility of eye-gaze (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 2001; Kano et al., 2021) (also see Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: H3 (perceptual advantage of the horizontally elongated eye shape) cannot explain the results.
source: H3 (perceptual advantage of the horizontally elongated eye shape) also cannot explain our results likely because small variations in the horizontal eye length do not critically affect the visibility of eye-gaze.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: Humans can take more extreme sideway eye positions than chimpanzees due to their horizontally elongated eye shape.
source: However, it should be noted that humans can take more extreme sideway eye positions than chimpanzees due to their horizontally elongated eye shape (Kobayashi and Kohshima, 2001), and such mechanistic difference may be one advantage of the human eye in eye-gaze signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The majority of eye positions fall within 20° in both chimpanzees and humans in naturalistic conditions.
source: Yet, this fact might be of limited relevance to real-life social interaction because previous eye-tracking studies measuring eye movements of chimpanzees and humans in naturalistic conditions indicated that the majority of eye positions fall within 20°, the eye position adopted in our stimuli, in both species (Kano and Tomonaga, 2013; Kothari et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous eye-tracking studies.

claim: H4 and H5 (perceptual expertise in own-species and normal eye contrast polarity) cannot largely explain the results.
source: H4 and H5 (perceptual expertise in own-species and normal eye contrast polarity) also cannot largely explain our results.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results in relation to the hypotheses.

claim: The presence of the uniformly white sclera in the stimuli is the primary factor affecting the similarity of results between the participants of both species.
source: Overall, however, our results indicate that the presence of the uniformly white sclera (and a darker iris) in our stimuli is the primary factor affecting the similarity of our results between the participants of both species in our study design.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: The visibility of human eye-gaze is primarily supported by basic color properties of the eyes, and thus by a basic perceptual mechanism shared among human and chimpanzee participants.
source: Our results thus suggest that the visibility of human eye-gaze is primarily supported by basic color properties of the eyes, and thus by a basic perceptual mechanism shared among human and chimpanzee participants.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results.

claim: There are similarities in visual perception, including spectrum sensitivity, visual acuity, and contrast sensitivity, between humans and nonhuman apes.
source: Relatedly, there are a number of previous studies documenting the similarities in visual perception, including spectrum sensitivity, visual acuity, and contrast sensitivity, between humans and nonhuman apes (Deeb et al., 1994; Dulai et al., 1994; Jacobs et al., 1996; Matsuno et al., 2004; Matsuno and Tomonaga, 2006; Matsuzawa, 1990; Bard et al., 1995; Adams et al., 2017) though small differences might exist (Jacobs et al., 1996; Adams et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Chimpanzees required extensive training to distinguish between different gaze directions of human and chimpanzee eyes.
source: One notable aspect of our results is that chimpanzees required extensive training to distinguish between different gaze directions of human and chimpanzee eyes, and many of our chimpanzees were unable to pass all the required training phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the training phase.

claim: Many chimpanzees were unable to pass all the required training phases.
source: One notable aspect of our results is that chimpanzees required extensive training to distinguish between different gaze directions of human and chimpanzee eyes, and many of our chimpanzees were unable to pass all the required training phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the training phase.

claim: Chimpanzees may generally find it more difficult attending to detailed perceptual features of the eyes compared to humans.
source: Given that many of our chimpanzees were already trained for simple color and form perception tasks (e.g., Matsuno et al., 2004; Matsuzawa, 1990), this difficulty might suggest that chimpanzees may generally find it more difficult attending to detailed perceptual features of the eyes compared to humans, consistent with the previous training (Tomonaga and Imura, 2010) and gaze-following/cueing studies (Tomasello et al., 2007; Tomonaga, 2007; but see Povinelli and Eddy, 1996).
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Gaze perception in humans is supported by both the uniformly white sclera of eyes and their perceptual expertise in such detailed eye features.
source: In this sense, consistent with the previous experimental studies in humans (Tomasello et al., 2007; Whalen et al., 2004; Provine et al., 2013b; Ricciardelli et al., 2000), our results also suggest that gaze perception in humans is supported by both the uniformly white sclera of eyes and their perceptual expertise in such detailed eye features.
evidence: This claim is an inference from the experimental results and previous studies.

claim: Only a small number of chimpanzees could participate in the test conditions, which hampers the generalization of the results.
source: One clear limitation of this study is that only a small number of chimpanzees could participate in our test conditions, which hampers the generalization of our results.
evidence: This claim acknowledges a limitation of the study based on the experimental data.

claim: If the performance of the current task is supported by simple color properties of eyes and basic visual perception of great apes, the results should be replicated in other (trained) individuals and likely also in other great ape species.
source: Nonetheless, if the performance of the current task is supported by simple color properties of eyes and basic visual perception of great apes as argued above, our results should be replicated in other (trained) individuals and likely also in other great ape species.
evidence: This claim is a speculation about the generalizability of the results.

claim: Some chimpanzee individuals have partly unpigmented (white) sclera.
source: Finally, it remains unanswered whether our results are generalizable to other stimuli with some variations in sclera color, specifically given that some chimpanzee individuals have partly unpigmented (white) sclera (Perea-García et al., 2019; Caspar et al., 2021; Mearing and Koops, 2021; Kano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous morphological studies.

claim: Partly unpigmented sclera in chimpanzees is typically characterized as more graded or patchy compared to humans' uniformly white sclera.
source: However, such sclera is typically characterized as more graded or patchy compared to humans' uniformly white sclera.
evidence: This claim is based on morphological observations from previous studies.

claim: The visibility of eye-gaze (especially that of eye-outline edges) is limited with the eyes of all nonhuman ape species without the human-like uniformly white sclera, particularly in visually challenging conditions.
source: Moreover, as noted earlier, the previous simulation study demonstrated that the visibility of eye-gaze (especially that of eye-outline edges) is limited with the eyes of all nonhuman ape species without the human-like uniformly white sclera, particularly in visually challenging conditions (Kano et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous simulation study.

claim: The study demonstrated that uniform whiteness in the exposed sclera enhances eye-gaze signaling.
source: In conclusion, we demonstrated that uniform whiteness in the exposed sclera enhances eye-gaze signaling.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The study provided experimental support for the gaze-signaling hypothesis despite recent criticisms.
source: We thus provided experimental support for the gaze-signaling hypothesis despite recent criticisms on this hypothesis (Perea-García et al., 2019; Caspar et al., 2021; Mearing and Koops, 2021).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion from the experimental data in relation to the hypothesis.

claim: It is the uniformly white sclera but not necessarily other distinguishing features that critically distinguishes the human eye from the chimpanzee eye in terms of the visibility of eye-gaze direction.
source: Specifically, we found that it is the uniformly white sclera but not necessarily other distinguishing features, such as iris-sclera color difference and some variation in horizontal eye elongation, that critically distinguishes the human eye from the chimpanzee eye in terms of the visibility of eye-gaze direction.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: One function of the uniformly white sclera is to equip the eye-gaze signal with robustness against degradation caused by natural noises.
source: Moreover, we found that one function of the uniformly white sclera is to equip the eye-gaze signal with robustness against degradation caused by natural noises (e.g., shading, distancing).
evidence: This claim is a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Humans have evolved special external eye morphology for conspecific communication.
source: These new findings, when combined with the original and related hypotheses, suggest that humans have evolved special external eye morphology for conspecific communication and that it is a vital part of communication for humans to read conspecific eye-gaze cues during their everyday cooperative and cultural activities.
evidence: This claim is a speculation based on the experimental findings and previous hypotheses.

claim: It is a vital part of communication for humans to read conspecific eye-gaze cues during their everyday cooperative and cultural activities.

claim: Study 1 tested 25 human adults who had moderate to extensive experience in caretaking or studying chimpanzees.
source: Study 1 tested 25 human adults (14 females, 11 males; 23 East/South Asians and 1 Caucasian male) who had moderate to extensive experience in caretaking or studying chimpanzees (3 months = 1; 1–5 years = 10; 5–10 years = 4; >10 years = 10).
evidence: This claim describes the participant characteristics in the study.

claim: The iris-sclera color differences did not significantly differ between human and chimpanzee stimuli with both normal and reversed contrast polarities.
source: We confirmed that, as found in a previous study (Kano et al., 2021), the iris-sclera color differences did not significantly differ between our human and chimpanzee stimuli (with both normal and reversed contrast polarities; Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by image analysis data and references a figure.

claim: The human eye was horizontally longer than the chimpanzee eye in the stimuli.
source: We confirmed that, as found in the previous study (Kano et al., 2021), the human eye was horizontally longer than the chimpanzee eye, but the size of the sclera ROI did not differ between the human and chimpanzee eye in our stimuli (Appendix 3—figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by image analysis data and references a figure.
